Quantitative equity research · Backtest study

Market-Neutral Reversal Book

A dollar-, beta- and sector-neutral US equity strategy that blends three weakly correlated forecasting sleeves, sized to a risk target and charged a full execution-cost model on every trade.

01 What the strategy does

The book is a cross-sectional bet. It never takes a view on whether the market goes up or down. Every trading day it scores each stock in its universe relative to the others, buys the names with the highest scores and shorts the names with the lowest, in sizes that make the long and short legs cancel out. What remains is a bet purely on the ordering of stocks against each other.

Three independent forecasts drive that ordering, and each rests on a different economic mechanism:

  • Volume-shock reversal. When a stock moves sharply on unusually heavy volume, the move is often somebody demanding liquidity in a hurry rather than new information arriving. Dealers who absorb that order are compensated when the price drifts back. The sleeve buys recent losers and sells recent winners, scaled by how unusual the volume behind the move was, so it tilts toward the liquidity-driven half of the moves rather than the informed half.
  • Overnight reversal. The overnight session is thin and order-driven, and prices that gap on it tend to give part of the gap back during the following day. This is a genuinely different bet from total-return reversal — the two correlate at only 0.30.
  • Earnings surprise. When a company reports earnings far from what its own history implied, the price keeps drifting in the direction of the surprise for weeks afterwards rather than adjusting at once. The sleeve measures each quarter's earnings against the same quarter a year earlier, scaled by how variable those surprises usually are for that company, and fades the score to zero over the following 60 trading days.

The three scores are standardized and blended, then handed to a risk pipeline that decides position sizes, enforces neutrality and applies hard limits. The resulting target weights are traded at the next day's open and held for ten trading days.

Why blend rather than pick the best? A single sleeve is capped by how many genuinely independent bets it can make. Combining forecasts that are nearly uncorrelated raises the information ratio roughly with the square root of the number of independent views. Blending volume-shock reversal with overnight reversal lifted gross Sharpe from 0.68 to 0.91 — the largest single gain in the project — and adding earnings surprise takes out-of-sample net Sharpe from 0.63 to 0.91. Both out-of-sample numbers come from the same validation harness, so the increment is the sleeve and not a change of method.

02 The pipeline, stage by stage

These four stages run in order, and each is independently testable. The sequence matters: the signal knows nothing about risk, the risk model knows nothing about cost, and the execution layer is the only place where money actually changes hands.

1

Signal construction

Each sleeve is computed from data through the day's close, masked to the tradable universe, clipped at ±3 median-absolute-deviations to tame outliers, then standardized cross-sectionally to mean zero and unit dispersion. Standardizing before blending is what makes the blend meaningful — raw momentum is of order 0.3 and raw two-day reversal of order 0.01, so combining the raw numbers would hand the entire book to whichever sleeve happens to have the larger units.

in: prices, volume, SEC filings → out: date × ticker score matrix
2

Risk model and position sizing

A Ledoit–Wolf shrunk covariance matrix is estimated over the tradable names on a 252-day window, refreshed monthly. Positions are sized inversely to volatility with direction and magnitude from the score, then scaled so the portfolio's ex-ante annualized volatility hits its target.

in: scores, returns → out: unconstrained target weights
3

Neutralization and constraints

Dollar, beta and sector neutrality are imposed as a single orthogonal projection rather than one after another — demeaning to get dollar neutrality would destroy beta neutrality and vice versa, so they must be solved together. Position caps and a liquidity limit are then applied, and because clipping breaks neutrality while re-projecting breaks the caps, the two alternate to a fixed point before a final uniform down-scale makes every limit hold exactly.

in: target weights → out: constrained, neutral weights
4

Execution and cost accounting

Weights formed at the day-t close are traded at the t+1 open and held to the t+2 open. Every trade pays commission, regulatory fees and slippage; every short pays borrow each day it is open. Trades below a no-trade band or below the size that clears the per-order commission minimum are skipped entirely.

in: weights, prices → out: daily P&L, trade log, cost breakdown

03 Universe and data

The tradable universe is the 100 most liquid US large-cap common stocks, selected each month by trailing 63-day average dollar volume from current S&P 500 membership. Membership is held fixed between monthly refreshes: re-ranking daily would churn the book at the universe boundary for no forecasting reason.

Selection uses only information available before the day being selected for. Average dollar volume is lagged one bar, eligibility screens use lagged prices, and names must have at least 252 bars of history and trade above $5.

SourceWhat it providesCoveragePoint-in-time handling
yfinanceDaily OHLCV, split/dividend adjusted 496 tickers · 2,516 days Signals use data through the day's close; execution lagged one bar
SEC XBRLQuarterly and annual financial statement facts 503 tickers · 138,678 facts Each fact carries its filing date; visible only on and after that date
WikipediaS&P 500 membership and GICS sectors 503 tickers Current snapshot — see limitations
IBKR (ibapi)Hourly bars, for an intraday feasibility study 59 tickers · 309,573 bars Research only; not used by the production strategy

The filing date is what makes fundamentals honest. A company's December-quarter figures have a period end of 31 December but are not public until the report is filed in February. Ranking stocks on them in January would be trading on information nobody had. The common workaround is to lag all accounting data by six months, which is safe but discards months of genuinely available information. Because the SEC stamps every fact with its filing date, a value here becomes visible on the exact day it was filed and not before. Restatements handle themselves: a company that refiles 2019 numbers in 2021 produces a second fact with a later filing date, so a 2019 query still returns what the market actually had in 2019.

One unit choice worth flagging. Borrow is an annual rate but the engine only steps on trading days, so it is divided by 252 rather than 360. Charging a calendar-day rate on trading days only would under-bill the short leg by about 30%. Similarly the per-order commission minimum is denominated in dollars, not basis points, which is why NAV has to be tracked in levels rather than the backtest running purely in return space.

06 Results

The drawdown panel is the honest half of the chart. The worst decline is only 5.1%, but it took 438 trading days — most of two years — to recover, and the book spends long stretches underwater. A rising line hides that; an investor living through 2022 would not have experienced it as a steady climb.

Capital size is a real constraint, in both directions. A small account cannot run this strategy at all: at $10,000 with a hundred names the positions would be about $100 each, no trade would clear the $200 minimum size, and the book would never trade. The fixed per-order commission is what bites on the way down — net Sharpe is 0.95 at $1m and 0.89 at $100,000, where commission has risen from 14 to 38 bps a year.

Above the sweet spot the binding constraint changes from fixed costs to market impact. $1m scores better than $10m (0.954 against 0.938) because it consumes a tenth as much of each name's daily volume — 0.004% against 0.036% — so it pays less impact. The strategy has a capacity range, not a monotone preference for size.

07 Diagnosing the result

The Fundamental Law of Active Management decomposes an information ratio into three measurable terms: IR = TC × IC × √BR, where IC is forecasting skill, BR is the number of independent bets per year, and TC is the fraction of the ideal position that actually survives constraints and costs. Used as an instrument rather than decoration, it says where a result comes from and what would change it.

TermMeasuredInterpretation
IC (information coefficient)0.0113 Daily rank correlation between forecast and the return actually traded; t = 2.55
IC hit rate50.8% Share of days the forecast points the right way — barely above a coin flip, and enough
Naive breadth25,193 100 names × 252 days, if every name-day were an independent bet
Independent directions24.6 Of 100 names, after accounting for how correlated their residual returns are
Signal autocorrelation0.652 Holding a similar tilt for days is not a fresh bet each day
Effective breadth1,309 19× fewer independent bets per year than the naive count implies
TC from constraints0.631 Correlation between ideal and delivered weights
TC from costs0.829 Net Sharpe ÷ gross Sharpe — the fraction of edge surviving trading

08 Validation

A backtest is a claim about the future made from the past, and the ways it lies are well catalogued. Five controls run against this one, and the headline number quoted throughout is the walk-forward result — every tunable parameter is re-selected on each fold's training window, so nothing is chosen with hindsight.

ControlValueWhat it tests
Walk-forward OOS Sharpe0.912 Performance with every parameter chosen from past data only
Fixed-default OOS Sharpe0.951 Same windows, defaults fixed. Higher, but the defaults were chosen with full-sample hindsight — an optimistic reference, not an estimate
Train minus test+0.175 Size of the overfitting premium, in Sharpe units
Folds positive11 of 13 Whether the result is sustained or one lucky period
Probabilistic Sharpe0.991 Probability the true Sharpe exceeds zero, correcting for skew and fat tails
Deflated Sharpe (443 trials)0.671 The same, after discounting for every configuration examined
Min. track record length802 days History needed to call this Sharpe significantly positive; we have 1,638
PBO0.244 Probability that picking on in-sample rank is worse than a coin flip
Bootstrap 95% CI[0.23, 1.60] Sampling uncertainty around the out-of-sample estimate
Cost break-even6.43× How wrong the cost model can be before the edge disappears

Every configuration examined is counted. The Deflated Sharpe Ratio discounts a result for the number of things tried, and it only works if the count is honest. All 443 configurations touched across the project — including exploratory sweeps and every rejected candidate — are fed in, because a parameter chosen by looking at results is a trial whether or not it ran inside the reported script. The count lives in a tracked ledger on disk rather than in anyone's memory: a remembered trial count only ever drifts downward, in exactly the direction that flatters the result.

Engine verification

Two checks run against the backtester itself, independent of any strategy result. With no-trade bands disabled the engine fully rebalances each day, so its gross return must equal a one-line vectorized expression that shares no code with it; they agree to 1×10⁻¹⁷. And shifting the weights a day in either direction must move the result violently — a backtest that scores the same whether it trades on yesterday's, today's or tomorrow's signal is not using the timing it claims.

09 Challenges and how they were resolved

These are the problems that actually cost time, in the order they were hit. Several were silent — no error, just quietly wrong numbers — and the diagnostics that caught them turned out to be more valuable than the fixes.

Silent data corruption

The price cache never hit, then poisoned itself

Symptom
Gross Sharpe fell from 0.64 to 0.16 with no modelling change to explain it. Considerable time went into blaming the covariance estimator.
Cause
Two compounding bugs. The cache filename came from Python's hash() on strings, which is randomized per process — so the key differed every run, the cache never hit, and the full panel was re-downloaded each time (14 duplicate files, 620 MB). That eventually triggered rate limiting, and a throttled response comes back structurally complete and almost entirely empty. It was written to cache, and the reuse check matched on column names, so the empty panel was then served to every later run.
Fix
A stable sha1 key; coverage measured on non-null rows rather than column presence; and a refusal to cache any download covering under 80% of requested tickers. Both bugs now have regression tests.
Lesson
When a metric moves and no code change explains it, check the data first — shape, density, ticker count — before bisecting logic. The diagnostic that found it was one line: the fraction of non-null prices in the panel.
Look-ahead bias

A causality test caught a leak introduced by an optimization

Symptom
A test asserting that truncating the price panel leaves every earlier weight unchanged began failing.
Cause
An attempt to estimate the covariance matrix over "every name ever in the universe" — a set only knowable at the end of the backtest. The shrinkage intensity therefore depended on future membership.
Fix
Estimate over the names tradable on each refresh day, which is both causal and better calibrated. Names joining mid-period wait for the next refresh rather than borrowing an invented estimate.
Lesson
The causality test is load-bearing for the whole validation harness: the walk-forward runs each configuration once and slices it per fold, which is only valid because the pipeline is causal. If that test breaks, every out-of-sample number silently becomes in-sample.
Hindsight in the defaults

Out-of-sample numbers that were quietly in-sample

Symptom
Out-of-sample Sharpe of 0.19 looked reasonable while a fixed-defaults comparison scored 0.34 — the defaults beating per-fold selection by a suspicious margin.
Cause
The holding period had been chosen by looking at full-sample results and then pinned in the config. Every fold inherited that hindsight. Separately, the "fixed defaults" comparison column was not reading the defaults at all: with a non-empty sweep grid there was no entry named base, so the code silently fell back to the first grid cell, which happened to be the worst configuration.
Fix
Every selectable parameter moved into the walk-forward grid, so each fold re-chooses it from training data. The comparison column now always evaluates the true base configuration. Honest out-of-sample Sharpe dropped to 0.05 — a far more useful number than the 0.19 it replaced.
Lesson
Any parameter chosen by looking at results belongs in the validation grid, not the config file. Pinning it is how an out-of-sample number stops being out-of-sample without anyone noticing.
Hindsight, second time

The same mistake survived the fix, and the trial count drifted

Symptom
A review of the finished project found the documentation saying the reversal lookback k was re-selected per fold, while the walk-forward grid did not contain it. Separately, the trial count was quoted as 327 while the ledger on disk summed to 299.
Cause
k = 2 had been chosen from a full-sample IC sweep and stayed pinned in the config through both phases, so every fold inherited it. The count was inflated by double-counting: the headline grid was in the ledger and added again by the run, and the defaults — already a grid cell — were run and counted a second time under the label base.
Fix
k joined the grid at the specification's pre-registered values {1, 2, 3, 5, 10}, not a range centred on the number already picked, taking it to 135 cells. The run cache now counts distinct configurations, the ledger marks earlier grids that the new one contains as superseded, and the embargo covers the longest holding period anywhere in the grid rather than the default's. The out-of-sample result held: folds chose k = 2 on their own in 11 of 13.
Lesson
A fix described in prose is not a fix verified in code. The README and this write-up are now checked by a test against the numbers the last run wrote, and the trial ledger lives in version control rather than in a git-ignored output folder.
Cost modelling

Spread estimators that do not work at this liquidity

Symptom
With per-name spreads estimated from daily bars, the strategy was unprofitable at every universe size tested.
Cause
Two standard estimators were tried — Corwin–Schultz (2012) and Abdi–Ranaldo (2017) — and both fail badly here. Against mega-caps whose true half-spreads are common knowledge (roughly 0.3–0.5 bps), they returned 0.00 and 4.91 bps for Apple, 4.73 and 19.90 for Microsoft. Both infer the spread from the geometry of the daily range, and when the spread is 0.3 bps against 150 bps of daily volatility there is nothing to recover — they measure volatility.
Fix
A calibrated function of dollar volume, 56 × ADV$m−0.735, anchored to published spread levels and honest about being an assumption. It puts this universe at 0.44 bps median — revealing that the flat 2 bps originally assumed was about 4.5× too expensive, not too cheap.
Lesson
A principled estimator applied outside its regime is worse than a transparent assumption. The bar-based estimators were designed for markets where the spread is a material fraction of daily movement; modern US mega-caps are the opposite case. The cost-sensitivity sweep now carries the residual uncertainty.
Constraint interaction

The volatility target cannot be reached, and that is arithmetic

Symptom
Ex-ante volatility settles near 3.3% against a 10% target, no matter how the signal is configured.
Cause
A dollar-neutral book of N names capped at w each can carry at most about w · σidio · √N of volatility. At a 1.5% cap and 100 names that ceiling is roughly 3.5%. The two settings are mutually inconsistent; the cap binds first and always will.
Fix
Stated explicitly in the generated report rather than left implicit in a diagnostics table. Sharpe is scale-invariant so the ratio is unaffected, but realized return is proportionally smaller and the fixed per-order commission minimum weighs more heavily on the smaller book.
Lesson
Two limits set independently will often contradict each other. A diagnostic that reports which constraint is actually binding is worth more than either limit on its own.
Counterintuitive result

Loosening constraints made everything worse

Symptom
The transfer coefficient sits at 0.63, implying more than a third of the ideal alpha is lost to portfolio construction. Raising it seemed like free performance.
Cause
Nothing was broken. Raising the transfer coefficient from 0.63 to 0.84 — looser position caps, dropping sector neutrality, mean-variance weights — lowered net Sharpe from 0.78 to 0.39, and gross Sharpe fell too, so it was not merely the extra turnover.
Fix
Left alone, with the finding documented. The constraints act as regularization: the "ideal" weights are built from a noisy alpha estimate, and caps stop the book concentrating wherever the noise happens to point. This is the Jagannathan–Ma (2003) result that imposing the wrong constraints helps.
Lesson
The Fundamental Law writes IR = TC · IC · √BR, which reads as though the transfer coefficient is a multiplier to maximize. That holds only when alpha is estimated without error. With a noisy forecast, the constraint that lowers TC also lowers the variance of what gets implemented, and the net effect can be — and here is — positive.
Negative result

Independence without breadth buys nothing

Symptom
Six value and quality sleeves built on point-in-time SEC data proved beautifully independent of the price sleeves — correlations of 0.00 to 0.03 — and none of them improved the blend at any weight tested.
Cause
Every one has an autocorrelation between 0.997 and 0.9995. Filings arrive four times a year and the ratio then sits still, so the signal delivers a handful of independent bets annually. Since IR = IC·√BR, the contribution is capped near zero regardless of how good the IC is: earnings yield has genuinely significant forecasting power and a negative standalone Sharpe.
Fix
Reframed the search from independence to independence with an event clock. An earnings surprise is not a level — it arrives, decays, and fiscal calendars are staggered across names, so the cross-section keeps turning over. That one sleeve does work, and carries 10% of the blend.
Lesson
Two signals built from the same filings, one useless and one useful, and the entire difference is breadth. This was the clearest demonstration in the project that the Fundamental Law earns its place as a measuring instrument.
Scope

Three data sources tried before one worked

Symptom
Fundamental signals need a decade of history with filing dates. The obvious sources do not provide it.
Cause
Interactive Brokers refuses fundamental data without a paid Reuters subscription (error 10358), though it serves historical bars without complaint. yfinance returns only five to seven quarters — nowhere near enough.
Fix
The SEC's XBRL API: free, official, back to 2009, no key required, and every fact carries its filing date. 138,678 facts across 503 tickers, with assets and equity covering all 503.
Lesson
The free source turned out to be strictly better than the paid one for this purpose, because filing dates make point-in-time discipline exact rather than approximate.

10 Extension: three directions, two dead ends

A second round of work targeted the term the Fundamental Law identified as binding — the number of independent bets. Three directions were tried in order of how much new information each brought, rather than how promising each looked, because the Deflated Sharpe charges for search but not for evidence. Net out-of-sample Sharpe moved from 0.84 to 0.90, and the gain came from none of the three.

Direction A · rejected

Insider filings and further earnings cuts

Idea
If an earnings surprise earns its place because it has an event clock, find more event clocks. Six candidates: four built on SEC Form 4 insider filings (217,517 open-market trades, median filing lag of exactly 2 days, as the statute requires) and two further cuts of the existing XBRL panel.
Result
All six failed the inclusion gate. Insider net buying has significantly negative forecasting power in this universe — IC −0.0133 at t = −3.50.
Judgement
The sign was not flipped. It survived two artefact checks (only 1.7% of scored days are zero-filled; restricting to names that actually filed within 60 days gives −0.0145, t = −3.66), but the literature's prior is positive and there is no mechanism for a negative one. Reversing a sign because one sample says so is the exact curve-fit this project exists to detect. Revenue surprise had the best IC ever measured here (0.0175, t = 3.05) and was still rejected: at 0.46 correlation with the existing earnings sleeve it is a redundant variant, not a new bet.
Direction B · rejected at the gate

Passive execution, killed by one line of arithmetic

Idea
Hourly reversal carries roughly twenty times the effective breadth of the daily signal. It was unaffordable because crossing the spread on that much turnover costs more than the edge. But a resting limit order earns the half-spread rather than paying it — so the dominant cost might change sign rather than merely shrink.
Result
A parametric fill-quality map killed it before any microstructure work: commission + fees = 0.700 bps per dollar traded against a maximum spread capture of 0.440 bps. Even with flawless passive fills and zero adverse selection, each dollar traded still costs 0.26 bps.
Judgement
Turnover never becomes free, so the twentyfold breadth cannot be bought. The thesis rested on a cost structure this project had already disproved — once the spread was calibrated at 0.44 bps rather than assumed at 2, commission, not spread, became the dominant per-dollar cost, and earning the spread cannot flip a sign commission controls. Two hours of arithmetic replaced a multi-week simulation.
Direction C · rejected, but it found the lever

Regime conditioning, and the control that exposed it

Idea
Blend IC across quartiles of cross-sectional dispersion is monotone (−0.003, +0.008, +0.018, +0.024) and the mechanism fits — reversal is paid for providing liquidity, and both reversal sleeves strengthen with dispersion while the earnings sleeve shows no pattern at all. So scale risk with the regime.
Result
It improved the number for the wrong reason. A constant multiplier at the same average size beat the regime-varying one (0.907 against 0.878), and the diagnostic found no alpha timing whatsoever — the return gap between scaled-up and scaled-down days was −0.000004. The entire gain was reduced turnover wearing a regime costume.
Judgement
Chasing the real mechanism found the actual lever: the no-trade band, which needed re-tuning once the sleeve set had changed. It is a genuine interior optimum, and the cliff is mechanically explained — a band wider than the 1.5% per-name cap means no trade can ever clear it.
No-trade band0.0000.003 0.0060.0100.0130.016+
net Sharpe0.8450.864 0.9380.9750.857 nothing trades

Two methodology upgrades came with this round. The walk-forward now embargoes the ten-day holding period off the end of each training window, so a position opened in training cannot still be open in the test window — without it, train and test share outcomes and the generalisation gap is flattered. And the trial count now lives in a ledger on disk, results/trial_ledger.json, under version control: every sweep with what it tried and what came of it, rejected candidates included, read automatically whenever a Sharpe is deflated.

11 Directions explored and closed

Three substantial lines of investigation did not make it into the strategy. Each was measured rather than assumed, and the measurement is the useful part.

Intraday horizons

Breadth is the binding constraint everywhere in this project, and hourly bars are where breadth lives. On 309,573 hourly bars pulled from Interactive Brokers, hourly reversal shows an IC of 0.0095 at t = 2.9 with an autocorrelation of −0.001 — every bar a genuinely fresh bet. That is 26,059 effective bets per year against 1,309 for the daily strategy, twenty times more.

The cost of collecting it is larger than the gain. At the measured transfer coefficient the implied gross information ratio is 0.97, and break-even requires trading under 12.5% of the book per bar; even at 2% per bar the implied result does not beat what the daily strategy already delivers. The conclusion is that intraday is viable only for an operator who can execute passively — earning the spread with limit orders rather than paying it, which reverses the sign of the dominant cost term. That is a different project, and this remains a diagnostic rather than a backtest.

12 Limitations

Every item here makes the true result worse than the reported one. None is hidden in an appendix because each changes how the numbers should be read.

Survivorship bias. The universe is seeded from current S&P 500 membership, and yfinance serves only currently-listed tickers, so companies that fell far enough to be delisted are absent from the entire history. For a reversal strategy the direction of this bias is unambiguous: the missing names are disproportionately those whose "oversold, buy it" signal never reverted. The reported results should be read as an upper bound. Fixing it properly needs a point-in-time constituent source or a delisting-inclusive history.

  • Costs not modelled. Margin financing on the long leg beyond cash, which a book running 1.0× gross genuinely pays. Hard-to-borrow rates above general collateral — and a reversal signal most wants to short recent winners, which skew expensive to borrow, so the uniform rate is a floor. Fill uncertainty: every intended trade is assumed to execute in full at the modelled price.
  • The spread is calibrated, not measured. Without quote data or real fills, the half-spread comes from a function fitted to published levels. The impact coefficient is likewise assumed. This is why the break-even multiple of 6.43× carries more weight than the base case.
  • Ten years is one sample. 2015–2024 was a specific regime. The minimum track record length needed to call this Sharpe significantly positive is 802 trading days and we have 1,638 — comfortable, but not by an order of magnitude.
  • The sector map is a current snapshot. Companies change GICS classification; sector neutrality is imposed using today's labels applied backwards.
  • Backtested performance is not live performance. Which is precisely why the cost model and the overfitting controls carry most of the weight here, and why the out-of-sample number with its confidence interval is the only claim being made.

13 Reproducing this

The project is a Python package with 262 tests covering the signal, the neutralization algebra, the cost accounting and the point-in-time discipline. A synthetic data generator with deliberately planted effects lets the entire suite run offline and deterministically, and doubles as ground truth: if the pipeline cannot recover a known signal there, the bug is ours rather than the market's.

Every number in this document regenerates from the repository. The headline comes from quant-capstone run; every side study — liquidity deciles, sleeve surveys, the transfer-coefficient variants, the Phase 2 directions, the intraday diagnostic — is a module in quant_capstone/studies that pins the configuration it was originally run under. Their tables are committed under results/studies, and --check regenerates them all and diffs the result against what is committed. The cached market data is pinned too: results/data_manifest.json records the hash of every input file, so a re-download that moves the numbers is caught before anyone starts debugging the model.

CommandWhat it does
uv syncCreate the environment and install dependencies
uv run pytest262 tests, about 20 seconds, no network needed
uv run quant-capstone run --source syntheticFull pipeline offline against planted effects
uv run quant-capstone runThe headline study on real data; downloads and caches on first use
uv run quant-capstone study allRegenerate every side study and every figure in this document
uv run quant-capstone study --checkRegenerate the study tables and diff them against the committed ones
uv run quant-capstone bookAssemble this document from Report/src
uv run quant-capstone crosscheckVerify the engine against independent calculations

Built with numpy, pandas, scikit-learn and statsmodels. Price data from yfinance; fundamentals from the SEC XBRL API; hourly bars from Interactive Brokers via ibapi. All figures generated from the final configuration by quant-capstone study figures.
